hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-02.title: Push $b$ to its maximum
hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-02.body:
If $a>1$ and $b<2$, moving a small amount $\varepsilon$ from $a$ to $b$ leaves $a+b$ unchanged but increases $b+c$, which lowers the sum; the same works with $c$ in place of $a$. So the minimum has $b=2$ (then $a+c=3$).

Now the sum is $\frac1{a+2}+\frac1{c+2}=\frac{a+c+4}{(a+2)(c+2)}=\frac{7}{(a+2)(c+2)}$. With $(a+2)+(c+2)=7$ fixed, the product $(a+2)(c+2)$ is largest when $a=c=\frac32$, giving $\frac72\cdot\frac72=\frac{49}4$. The minimum is $\frac{7}{49/4}=\frac47$.

**Answer: $\frac47$**

hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-02.title: Convexity
hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-02.body:
Let $s=a+b$ and $t=b+c$. Then $s+t=5+b\le7$ and $\frac1s+\frac1t\ge\frac4{s+t}\ge\frac47$ by AM-HM, with equality at $b=2$, $s=t=\frac72$ (i.e. $a=c=\frac32$), which is allowed.

**Answer: $\frac47$**

hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-03.title: Check $\pi$ and nothing smaller
hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-03.body:
Since $\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x$ and cosine is even, $f(x+\pi)=\cos(-\cos x)=f(x)$, so $\pi$ is a period.

The value $\cos 1$ is the minimum of $f$ (since $|\cos x|\le1<\pi$ and cosine decreases on $[0,1]$), and $f(x)=\cos 1$ exactly when $\cos x=\pm1$, i.e. $x$ is a multiple of $\pi$. So the points where $f=\cos 1$ are spaced $\pi$ apart, and no period can be smaller than $\pi$.

**Answer: $\pi$**

hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-04.title: Pair up the numbers
hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-04.body:
Group the numbers into the 5 pairs $\{1,10\},\{2,9\},\{3,8\},\{4,7\},\{5,6\}$, each summing to $11$. A valid subset takes at most one number from each pair: nothing, the first, or the second -- $3$ choices. Total $3^5=243$.

**Answer: 243**

hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-05.title: Count edges
hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-05.body:
Every edge borders exactly two faces, which cannot both be triangles or both be squares, so each edge borders one triangle and one square. With $t$ triangles and $s$ squares, the number of edges equals $3t$ (counting via triangles) and also $4s$ (via squares). So $3t=4s$ and $t/s=\frac43$.

**Answer: $\frac43$**

hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-06.title: Circle and tangent line
hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-06.body:
The equation is $x^2+(y-\frac32)^2=\frac{13}4$: a circle with centre $(0,\frac32)$ and radius $\frac{\sqrt{13}}2$. Write $x=\frac{\sqrt{13}}2\cos\theta$, $y=\frac32+\frac{\sqrt{13}}2\sin\theta$. Then $x+y=\frac32+\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)\le\frac32+\frac{\sqrt{13}}2\sqrt2=\frac{3+\sqrt{26}}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{3+\sqrt{26}}2$**

hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-07.title: Parity
hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-07.body:
Number the stones $1$ to $15$. An odd number of stones between stones $i<j$ means $j-i-1$ is odd, i.e. $i$ and $j$ have the same parity. So all five marked stones are odd-numbered or all even-numbered. There are $\binom85=56$ ways with odd numbers ($8$ odd positions) and $\binom75=21$ with even ($7$ even positions). Total $56+21=77$.

**Answer: 77**

hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-08.title: Ratio of areas
hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-08.body:
The centres $X$ of circles of radius $1$ lying inside $ABC$ form a smaller equilateral triangle whose sides are $1$ unit from those of $ABC$. Moving each side in by $1$ reduces the height by $3$ (the inradius drops by $1$ and the height is $3\times$ inradius), so its height is $10$ and its area is $\frac{10^2}{\sqrt3}=\frac{100}{\sqrt3}$.

The circle contains $O$ exactly when $|XO|<1$, which is a disc of radius $1$ about $O$ (it lies inside the small triangle, whose inradius is $\frac{10}{3}>1$), with area $\pi$.

Probability $=\frac{\pi}{100/\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt3\,\pi}{100}$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt3\pi}{100}$**

hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-09.title: Bound and extremal sets
hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-09.body:
Let $n=26$. Split a convex set into its top, bottom, left and right parts (the points that are extreme in the corresponding direction). Each part has at most $n$ points (distinct $x$ or $y$ coordinates) and the four corners are each shared by two parts, so a convex set has at most $4n-4=100$ points. We need $4n-6=98$, i.e. two points fewer.

- Any $98$ of the $100$ points on the boundary of the square (those with $x$ or $y\in\{1,26\}$): $\binom{100}{98}=4950$ sets.
- Otherwise some point has both coordinates strictly between $1$ and $26$. One side cannot have just $n-2$ points then. If two opposite sides each have $n-1$ points we get the boundary of an $(n-1)\times n$ rectangle: $4$ sets. If two adjacent sides each have $n-1$ points we get the boundary of the square with $(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)$ removed and $(2,2)$ added, or a rotation: $4$ sets.

Total $4950+4+4=4958$.

**Answer: 4958**

hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-10.title: Telescoping
hmmt-nov-2009-gen1-10.body:
With $x=\left(\frac12\right)^{3^n}$ the factor is $1-x+x^2=\frac{1+x^3}{1+x}=\frac{1+(1/2)^{3^{n+1}}}{1+(1/2)^{3^n}}$. Define $a_n=1+(1/2)^{3^n}$; the product up to $N$ is $\frac{a_{N+1}}{a_0}$. As $N\to\infty$, $a_{N+1}\to1$ and $a_0=\frac32$, so the product is $\frac23$.

**Answer: $\frac23$**
